skills.name: Modals: obligation, advice and polite requests

note.text: Must and have to can express obligation; should usually gives advice. Could you and would you can introduce polite requests. A modal is followed by the base verb: she must read, not must reads or must to read. Must not means prohibition; do not have to means absence of necessity. Context matters because a word can have more than one use. State the intended meaning rather than treating all modals as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Must and have to can express obligation; should usually gives advice. Could you and would you can introduce polite requests. A modal is followed by the base verb: she must read, not must reads or must to read. Must not means prohibition; do not have to means absence of necessity. Context matters because a word can have more than one use. State the intended meaning rather than treating all modals as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: At a Buea library, Bih must return the book by the agreed date. A friend says she should keep a reading list: that is advice. Bih asks, Could you explain the renewal rule? This is a request, not a statement about past ability. A notice saying visitors do not have to buy a book does not forbid buying one.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Choose the meaning first, then the form. Check the base verb after a modal. When correcting a sentence, preserve whether the speaker intended a requirement, a suggestion, permission or prohibition. Do not replace must not with do not have to: that changes the meaning.
